title: ACSM Expert Consensus Statement on Exertional Heat Illness: Recognition, Management, and Return to Activity
publisher: Current Sports Medicine Reports (American College of Sports Medicine)
claims: Exertional heat stroke (EHS) is a true medical emergency with potential for organ injury and death; optimal management follows a synchronized chain of survival that promotes rapid recognition and management and communication between care teams.

Suspected EHS requires immediate action: stop activity to stop body heat generation, provide rapid total-body cooling and call for emergency medical support; delayed recognition and insufficient or delayed cooling can result in medical complications including death.

Subtle to profound central nervous system changes together with a rectal temperature above 40°C are the primary identifying signs of EHS; rectal temperature helps differentiate EHS from other causes of athlete collapse.

Cold water immersion has effective cooling rates with good clinical outcomes and is the preferred cooling strategy; when cold-water immersion is not possible, the athlete should be cooled using the fastest cooling technique available.

Most exertional heat illnesses can be prevented by recognizing and modifying well-described risk factors; EHS risk rises with increasing environmental heat stress and increasing physical activity intensity, and activity should be modified or canceled in environments associated with high risk.
Heat acclimatization reduces the risk of heat illness and improves physical performance in the heat.

After EHS or exertional heat injury, the medical team should deem the athlete clinically recovered before resuming physical activity; return should be progressively reintroduced over several weeks to months and individualized for each athlete.
